concepts.title: Goroutines: Lightweight Concurrent Functions
concepts.description: A goroutine is a function that runs concurrently with the rest of your program, scheduled by the Go runtime rather than the operating system -- understanding how cheap they are, and why the main goroutine exiting kills everything else, is the entry point into all of Go's concurrency model.
learningObjectives: Launch a goroutine with the `go` keyword and explain what actually happens when you do.
Explain why goroutines are described as 'lightweight' compared to OS threads, in concrete terms (stack size, scheduling).
Predict what happens to running goroutines when the main function returns.
Explain why a loop variable captured by a goroutine closure can produce surprising results, and how Go 1.22+ changed that.
Identify a goroutine leak: a goroutine that will never terminate because nothing will ever unblock it.

sections.heading: Starting a Goroutine
Concurrency vs. Parallelism: Go's Headline Design Goal
sections.body:
Go's designers were explicit, from the language's earliest talks, that its central goal was making **concurrency** easy to express -- and it's worth being precise about a distinction that's easy to blur: **concurrency is about structuring a program as multiple independently-progressing activities; parallelism is about actually running more than one of them at the exact same instant, on separate CPU cores.** A single-core machine can absolutely run a highly concurrent Go program -- dozens of goroutines, each making progress in small interleaved slices of time -- without ever executing two of them in parallel; the runtime is simply switching between them fast enough that they *appear* to make simultaneous progress. Parallelism, by contrast, requires actual hardware: multiple cores genuinely executing separate goroutines at the same physical moment. Go's famous slogan (borrowed and popularized by Rob Pike, one of the language's creators) is 'concurrency is not parallelism' -- concurrency is a way of *structuring* your program's logic around independent, communicating pieces; parallelism is an *optimization* that may or may not happen underneath that structure, depending on available hardware. You can write concurrent code with zero parallelism (one core), and you can also -- less usefully -- write parallel code with no meaningful concurrency (running the exact same fixed set of independent tasks over and over). Go is deliberately designed so that expressing the *concurrent structure* (independent goroutines, communicating over channels) is simple and cheap, and then the runtime decides how much of that structure actually executes in parallel, based on `GOMAXPROCS` and how many CPU cores are genuinely available -- you rarely need to think about parallelism directly; you think about concurrency, and parallelism is something the runtime opportunistically extracts from it.

Goroutines are managed entirely by the Go runtime's own scheduler, not directly by the operating system -- the OS has no idea individual goroutines exist at all; it only sees a handful of OS threads that the Go runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto. This is what people mean when they call goroutines 'lightweight' compared to OS threads, and it's worth being concrete about why: an OS thread typically reserves a large, fixed-size stack (often 1MB or more on many systems) the moment it's created, whether or not it ever needs that much. A goroutine starts with a tiny stack -- around 2KB -- that the Go runtime grows and shrinks dynamically as needed, by copying it to a larger allocation when it would otherwise overflow. The practical consequence: spinning up thousands, or even hundreds of thousands, of goroutines is routine and cheap in Go, where spinning up that many OS threads directly would exhaust memory and crush the OS scheduler in most environments. This is the concrete mechanism behind Go's reputation for handling huge numbers of concurrent connections or tasks without special tuning.

The Go runtime scheduler maps many goroutines onto a much smaller number of OS threads (roughly `GOMAXPROCS` of them, defaulting to the number of CPU cores), switching between goroutines cooperatively at function calls, channel operations, and other scheduling points -- this is often called an M:N scheduler (M goroutines onto N OS threads). When `GOMAXPROCS` is greater than 1 and more than one goroutine is simultaneously runnable, the scheduler genuinely runs them in parallel across separate cores; when it's 1, or only one goroutine is runnable at a time, you get concurrency (interleaved progress) without any actual parallelism, and your program's observable correctness should never depend on which of those two situations you happen to be in. You don't need to manage the goroutine-to-thread mapping yourself; the entire point is that you write concurrent code in terms of goroutines and channels, and let the runtime decide how much of it actually runs in parallel on the hardware it's given.

examples.title: main Returning Before a Goroutine Gets to Run
examples.explanation: As written, this program almost always prints only "main returning now" -- the anonymous goroutine is scheduled, but `main` typically reaches its own end and the whole process exits before the goroutine ever gets a turn to run at all. Uncommenting the `time.Sleep` line would very likely make the goroutine's print show up too, but that's not a real fix -- it's papering over the underlying issue by guessing at a delay long enough to usually work on your machine, in your test environment, under your current load. A slower machine, a busier CI runner, or a slightly heavier goroutine body could make even a 100ms sleep insufficient. The correct fix, shown in this module's sync.WaitGroup concept, replaces the guess with an actual synchronization signal that waits exactly as long as necessary -- no more, no less -- regardless of timing.

examples.title: The Loop-Variable-Capture Fix for Pre-1.22 Code
examples.explanation: Each goroutine's function literal declares its own parameter, also named `i` for clarity, and the call `(i)` at the very end passes the loop's current value of `i` as an argument at the exact moment that specific goroutine is launched -- before the loop moves on to the next iteration. This gives every goroutine its own independent copy of the value, sidestepping the historical shared-variable trap entirely, regardless of Go version. On Go 1.22+, this explicit parameter-passing is no longer strictly necessary -- the loop variable itself is now scoped per-iteration by the language -- but writing it this way remains completely correct and, arguably, still a clearer signal of intent to a reader who doesn't have the exact Go version memorized. sync.WaitGroup here (covered in depth later in this module) is what makes wg.Wait() block until all three goroutines have called wg.Done(), guaranteeing all three prints happen before the program exits -- without it, this would have the exact same 'main exits before goroutines run' problem as the previous example.

examples.title: A Goroutine Leak From an Unbuffered Channel With No Receiver
examples.explanation: When `fetchWithTimeout(true)` is called, it starts a goroutine that will eventually try to send `42` on `ch`, but the function itself takes the early-return path and returns an error *without ever executing* `<-ch`. `ch` is unbuffered, so the goroutine's send blocks until something receives -- and nothing ever will, since the function that owned `ch` has already returned and nothing else has a reference to that channel. That goroutine is now parked forever, for the entire remaining lifetime of the program: not crashed, not cleaned up by the garbage collector (it's technically still 'live,' just permanently stuck), simply leaked. Call this function from many requests in a long-running server and you accumulate one leaked, permanently-blocked goroutine per failing call -- a slow, silent memory and resource leak. A real fix needs the goroutine to have some way to give up too, typically via a buffered channel sized to hold one result (so the send never blocks even with no reader) or a `select` combined with a `context.Context` that gets cancelled, so the goroutine can bail out instead of blocking forever.

misconceptions.description: Calling `go someFunction()` runs someFunction() in the background but Go automatically makes sure it finishes before the program exits, similar to how a browser might finish an in-flight network request before closing a tab.
misconceptions.clarification: Go makes no such guarantee at all. The moment `main()` returns, the entire process terminates immediately, and any goroutines still running -- no matter how close they were to finishing -- are simply cut off mid-execution, with no cleanup, no completion, and no notification. There is nothing implicit protecting a goroutine's completion; if you need main to wait for a goroutine, you must say so explicitly, most commonly with a `sync.WaitGroup`, a channel receive, or another explicit synchronization mechanism -- silence on your part means 'don't wait,' not 'wait as needed.'

misconceptions.description: Goroutines that are stuck waiting forever (leaked) will eventually get cleaned up by Go's garbage collector, the same way an unused object with no references does.
misconceptions.clarification: The garbage collector reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable by anything -- but a leaked goroutine blocked on a channel operation is still considered 'live' and runnable by the Go runtime; it's simply waiting for an event (a send, a receive, a lock) that will never occur. Because it's still technically alive and schedulable, it is never a candidate for garbage collection, no matter how long it sits blocked -- it will remain parked, holding onto its stack and any resources it captured, for the entire remaining lifetime of the program. This is precisely why goroutine leaks are a genuine, cumulative operational problem in long-running services rather than something the runtime quietly cleans up on its own.

exercises.prompt: What is most likely to happen when this program runs, and why is the outcome not fully guaranteed by the code itself?
hints: Think about what main() actually waits for after starting the 5 goroutines -- is there any synchronization here at all?
The `go` keyword returns control to the next line immediately -- it does not pause main to let the goroutine run first.
Without a WaitGroup, channel, or any other synchronization, there's no guarantee any of the 5 goroutines get a chance to run before main returns and the process exits.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Most likely, the program prints only "main done", with none or only some of the 5 goroutine prints appearing, and in no guaranteed order even if some do appear. This is because main() has no synchronization forcing it to wait for the goroutines, so it typically reaches its end and the process exits before the scheduler gives any of them a turn to run.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each `go fmt.Println(...)` call starts a new goroutine and immediately returns control to the loop, without waiting for that goroutine to actually execute. After the loop finishes launching all 5, `main` immediately prints "main done" and returns -- and the instant main returns, the entire program exits, taking any still-pending goroutines down with it before they necessarily get a chance to run. In practice you might occasionally see one or two of the numbered prints sneak in, purely due to scheduling timing, but there is no guarantee of that, and no guarantee of any particular order among the ones that do print -- this exact unpredictability is the reason explicit synchronization (a sync.WaitGroup, covered later in this module) is needed whenever you actually need to wait for goroutines to finish.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to leave a running background goroutine that periodically sends heartbeat values on `ch`, but calling it always results in a goroutine that blocks forever on its very first send, leaking. Find and fix the bug (assume the caller genuinely never intends to read every single heartbeat -- it just wants to be able to read one occasionally without the sender getting stuck).
hints: `ch` is created with `make(chan int)` -- an unbuffered channel. What does an unbuffered send require in order to complete?

Between starting the heartbeat and the first `<-ch` read, main is doing other things (sleeping) and not reading. What is the background goroutine doing on its very first `ch <- count` during that time?

A buffered channel lets a send complete without a reader present, up to the buffer's capacity -- consider giving `ch` a small buffer so the sender never has to block waiting for a reader that isn't ready yet.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `ch` is unbuffered, so `ch <- count` can only complete at the exact moment some other goroutine is simultaneously executing `<-ch` -- with main asleep and not reading for the first 3 seconds, the very first send blocks indefinitely, and the goroutine never gets past its first iteration, effectively leaking (it's stuck forever if main never eventually reads, and even here it's needlessly stalled). The fix gives `ch` a buffer of 1 (`make(chan int, 1)`), so one send can complete and sit in the channel's buffer without any reader present, letting the sending goroutine keep making progress instead of blocking on every single send. The `select`/`default` combination goes a step further, making the send non-blocking entirely: if the buffer already holds an unread heartbeat, the goroutine drops the new one instead of piling up or blocking, which matches the stated intent that the caller only wants to read occasionally, not receive every single heartbeat ever sent.

assessments.prompt: Why are goroutines described as 'lightweight' compared to OS threads?
options: Goroutines don't actually run real code concurrently -- they're simulated sequentially by the runtime, so there's no real scheduling overhead at all.

Goroutines start with a small (around 2KB), dynamically-growable stack and are scheduled by the Go runtime onto a small number of OS threads, whereas OS threads typically reserve a large fixed-size stack (often 1MB+) and are scheduled directly by the operating system.
Goroutines are lightweight because Go silently limits every program to a maximum of a few dozen goroutines at once, keeping total resource usage low.
Goroutines use less memory because they cannot access any heap-allocated data, only their own local stack variables.
assessments.explanation: The concrete resource difference is stack size and who does the scheduling: a goroutine's stack starts tiny (~2KB) and grows/shrinks dynamically as needed, while a typical OS thread reserves a large, fixed-size stack upfront regardless of actual need. Combined with the Go runtime multiplexing many goroutines onto a much smaller number of real OS threads (an M:N scheduler), this is what makes spinning up thousands of goroutines cheap where spinning up thousands of OS threads would not be. Option A is wrong -- goroutines do run genuinely concurrently (and in parallel across multiple cores when GOMAXPROCS > 1), it's not a sequential simulation. Option C is wrong -- there's no such fixed cap; production Go programs routinely run into the hundreds of thousands of goroutines. Option D is wrong -- goroutines can access heap-allocated data exactly like any other Go code; that's unrelated to why they're lightweight.

assessments.prompt: Explain what a goroutine leak is, why the garbage collector can't fix it, and what kind of code pattern typically causes one.
assessments.modelAnswer: A goroutine leak is a goroutine that becomes permanently blocked -- almost always on a channel send or receive, or occasionally a lock, that will never be satisfied -- and therefore never terminates for the rest of the program's lifetime. This differs fundamentally from a memory leak caused by holding an unnecessary reference to an object: Go's garbage collector reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable by any live part of the program, but a leaked goroutine is not unreachable garbage from the runtime's point of view -- it's still a live, schedulable goroutine that is simply waiting on an event that will never arrive. Because it's technically still 'alive,' it is never eligible for garbage collection, no matter how long it sits blocked; it continues to consume its stack memory and hold onto any resources or references it captured, for as long as the process keeps running. The most common cause is a mismatch between a goroutine's channel operation and its counterpart: a goroutine trying to send on an unbuffered (or full) channel that nothing will ever read from again, typically because the receiving code path already returned early -- due to an error, a timeout, or a cancelled request -- without ever getting to the point where it reads from that channel. In a long-running server, this kind of leak compounds silently: every request that hits the buggy code path leaks one more permanently-blocked goroutine, and over time this can exhaust memory even though no individual leak looks dramatic on its own. The general defense is designing every goroutine with an explicit way to be released even on the not-so-happy paths -- via a context.Context that can be cancelled, a channel buffered generously enough that a send can't block, or a select statement offering an alternative path out -- rather than assuming the 'normal' completion path is the only one that will ever execute.

concepts.title: Channels and select
concepts.description: Channels are Go's built-in mechanism for goroutines to communicate and synchronize by passing values, and select lets a goroutine wait on multiple channel operations at once -- together they implement Go's famous slogan, "don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."
learningObjectives: Create and use both unbuffered and buffered channels, and explain the blocking behavior difference between them.
Close a channel with `close` and explain what happens when receiving from a closed channel, including the two-value receive form.
Use `select` to wait on multiple channel operations simultaneously, including a `default` case for non-blocking behavior.
Explain the deadlock that results from sending on (or receiving from) a channel with no corresponding goroutine on the other end.
Use a channel as a signal (e.g. `done chan struct{}`) rather than as a value-carrying pipe.

sections.heading: Channels: Typed Pipes Between Goroutines
sections.body:
A **channel** is a typed conduit that one goroutine can send values into and another can receive values from, created with `make(chan T)` for some type `T`:

```go
ch := make(chan int)

go func() {
	ch <- 42        // send: blocks until another goroutine receives
}()

value := <-ch     // receive: blocks until another goroutine sends
fmt.Println(value)   // 42
```

By default, a channel created with `make(chan int)` is **unbuffered**: a send (`ch <- value`) blocks the sending goroutine until some other goroutine performs a matching receive (`<-ch`), and symmetrically, a receive blocks until a send is ready. This is not a side effect or a limitation -- it's the core of how channels provide *synchronization*, not just data transfer: an unbuffered channel operation is a rendezvous point, a guarantee that both sides were actually present and ready at that instant, which is exactly what makes channels useful for coordinating goroutines, not merely passing values between them.

`make(chan int, 3)` creates a **buffered** channel with room for 3 values in flight. A send into a buffered channel that isn't full completes immediately, without waiting for a receiver -- only once the buffer is completely full does a further send block, waiting for some receive to make room. Buffering changes *when* blocking happens, but doesn't eliminate the possibility of blocking altogether; it's a tool for decoupling producer and consumer timing to a bounded degree, not a way to guarantee a send never waits.

sections.heading: Closing a Channel and the Two-Value Receive
sections.body:
`close(ch)` signals that no more values will ever be sent on a channel -- it's a one-way, one-time announcement from whoever owns the sending side (as a strong convention: **only the sender should ever close a channel**, never the receiver, since closing a channel that might still receive further sends elsewhere is a recipe for a panic). Receiving from a closed channel never blocks: it immediately returns the channel's zero value, forever, for every subsequent receive.

This creates an ambiguity a plain receive can't resolve on its own: did I get `0` because someone genuinely sent `0`, or because the channel is closed and has nothing left? The **two-value receive form** answers exactly this:

```go
value, ok := <-ch
// ok is true if value was an actual sent value
// ok is false if the channel is closed and drained -- value is the zero value
```

`for value := range ch` is the idiomatic way to drain a channel until it's closed: it automatically receives repeatedly and exits the loop cleanly the moment the channel is closed and empty, without you needing to check `ok` by hand on every iteration. One more sharp edge worth naming directly: **sending on an already-closed channel panics immediately**, and **closing an already-closed channel also panics** -- `close` is emphatically not idempotent, and there is no natural way to check 'is this channel already closed?' before closing it (checking via a receive would itself consume a value or race with other receivers). The discipline this demands is: have exactly one clear owner responsible for closing each channel, exactly once, only after that owner is certain no further sends will ever be attempted.

sections.heading: select: Waiting on Multiple Channels at Once
sections.body:
A single channel receive (`<-ch`) can only wait on one channel. `select` lets a goroutine wait on *several* channel operations simultaneously, proceeding with whichever one becomes ready first:

```go
select {
case msg := <-ch1:
	fmt.Println("from ch1:", msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
	fmt.Println("from ch2:", msg)
case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):
	fmt.Println("timed out waiting for either channel")
}
```

If more than one case is ready simultaneously, `select` picks one **at random** among the ready cases -- not top-to-bottom, not by any priority -- a deliberate design choice that prevents code from accidentally depending on case ordering and forces you to design each case as genuinely independent. `time.After(d)` is an extremely common idiom seen inside a `select`: it returns a channel that receives a single value after duration `d` has elapsed, letting you implement a timeout for 'wait for this channel, but give up after N seconds' entirely within the `select` itself, with no separate timer bookkeeping required.

Adding a `default` case makes the entire `select` **non-blocking**: if no other case is immediately ready, `default` runs right away instead of waiting for any of them. This is the standard way to attempt a send or receive 'if possible, otherwise move on' -- exactly the pattern used to make a channel send non-blocking when you'd rather drop a value than stall (as seen in the previous concept's heartbeat exercise).

sections.heading: Deadlock: Nobody Left to Meet the Rendezvous
Channels as Signals, Not Just Pipes
sections.body:
Not every channel exists to carry meaningful data -- a very common Go idiom uses a channel purely as a **signal**, where the fact that a receive succeeded (or that the channel was closed) is the entire message, and the value itself is irrelevant. `chan struct{}` is the idiomatic type for this: `struct{}` is the empty struct, which occupies zero bytes of memory, making it the natural 'I don't actually care about the payload, only the event' type.

```go
done := make(chan struct{})

go func() {
	doWork()
	close(done)   // signal: "I'm finished" -- the value never mattered, only the closing
}()

<-done   // blocks until doWork() has finished and done is closed
fmt.Println("worker finished")
```

Closing `done` (rather than sending a value into it) is a deliberate and common choice here specifically because closing broadcasts to *every* current and future receiver simultaneously and forever -- if multiple goroutines are all waiting on `<-done`, closing it releases all of them at once, whereas a single sent value would only satisfy one waiting receiver. This exact pattern -- an unbuffered or closed `chan struct{}` used purely as a completion/cancellation signal -- is also the conceptual seed of `context.Context`'s cancellation mechanism, which you'll encounter in later, more advanced material; internally, a cancelled context is implemented by closing exactly this kind of signal channel.

examples.title: Unbuffered vs. Buffered Send Blocking Behavior
examples.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	unbuffered := make(chan int)
	buffered := make(chan int, 2)

	buffered <- 1   // succeeds immediately -- buffer has room
	buffered <- 2   // succeeds immediately -- buffer now full (2/2)
	fmt.Println("both buffered sends completed without any receiver")

	go func() {
		fmt.Println(<-unbuffered)   // the receiver that makes the next line possible
	}()
	unbuffered <- 42   // blocks until the goroutine above is ready to receive
	fmt.Println("unbuffered send completed once a receiver showed up")
examples.explanation: The two sends into `buffered` both complete instantly with no receiver anywhere in sight, because the channel's buffer (capacity 2) has room for both values -- buffering lets a send succeed without a rendezvous, up to that capacity. `unbuffered`, by contrast, has zero buffer capacity, so `unbuffered <- 42` cannot proceed until some other goroutine is simultaneously ready to receive; that's exactly why the receiving goroutine is launched first, on the line above, so it's available to complete the rendezvous the moment the main goroutine's send is attempted. Without that goroutine existing at all, `unbuffered <- 42` in `main` -- the only goroutine -- would deadlock the entire program, exactly as shown in the deadlock explanation section.

examples.title: select With a Timeout via time.After
examples.explanation: `slowOperation` takes 3 seconds before it can send on `result`, but the `select` is only willing to wait 1 second, via the channel `time.After(1 * time.Second)` returns -- that channel receives exactly one value once its duration elapses, and nothing before that. Because the timeout case becomes ready well before `result` ever will, `select` picks the timeout branch and prints "gave up waiting after 1 second"; the still-running `slowOperation` goroutine eventually finishes its sleep and tries to send on `result` regardless, at which point (with no receiver left, since main's select already moved on and main will likely exit soon after) it may itself become a leaked goroutine if nothing ever drains `result` -- a good illustration that adding a timeout to a select solves the 'don't wait forever' problem for the goroutine doing the selecting, but doesn't automatically clean up whatever the abandoned goroutine on the other end is still doing.

examples.title: Broadcasting Completion With a Closed Signal Channel
examples.explanation: All three worker goroutines block on `<-done` at roughly the same time, each waiting for the signal channel to produce something. `close(done)` is what actually releases them -- and it releases *all three at once*, not just one, because a closed channel returns its zero value immediately and repeatedly to every current and future receiver, forever. If `done <- struct{}{}` had been used instead of closing (sending one signal value rather than closing the channel), only one of the three waiting goroutines would receive that single value; the other two would remain blocked indefinitely, since nothing else would ever be sent. This is exactly why 'close to broadcast a completion signal to everyone waiting' is the idiomatic pattern when multiple goroutines need to be released by the same event, rather than sending distinct values to each one individually.

misconceptions.description: Sending a value into a buffered channel, like `make(chan int, 5)`, never blocks -- that's the whole point of giving it a buffer.
misconceptions.clarification: A buffered channel only avoids blocking on a send while the buffer has free capacity. Once the buffer is completely full -- all 5 slots occupied by unreceived values, in this example -- the very next send blocks exactly like an unbuffered channel would, waiting until some goroutine performs a receive to free up a slot. Buffering shifts *when* blocking kicks in (after N values are already in flight, rather than immediately), and can smooth over short bursts of timing mismatch between producer and consumer, but it does not remove the possibility of blocking altogether for a producer that's consistently faster than its consumer.

misconceptions.description: If several goroutines are all blocked waiting to receive from a channel, and one goroutine sends a single value, all of the waiting goroutines receive a copy of that value.
misconceptions.clarification: A single sent value satisfies exactly one waiting receiver -- Go channels are point-to-point for actual sent values, not a broadcast mechanism; the runtime picks one of the waiting receivers to hand that value to, and the rest remain blocked, still waiting. Broadcasting to every current and future waiter simultaneously requires closing the channel instead of sending a value -- a closed channel returns its zero value to every receive, present and future, which is exactly the mechanism used for 'release everyone waiting on this signal at once,' as opposed to 'hand this one specific value to whichever one receiver happens to be selected.'

exercises.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
hints: The channel is buffered with room for 2, and exactly 2 values are sent before it's closed -- both sends should succeed without needing a receiver present yet.
`for v := range ch` keeps receiving until the channel is BOTH closed AND drained of any remaining buffered values -- closing alone doesn't discard values still sitting in the buffer.
Think about whether closing a channel that still has buffered values in it prevents those values from being received afterward.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 1, then 2, then "loop finished cleanly" -- with no panic and no deadlock. Closing a channel doesn't discard values already sitting in its buffer; range continues to receive those remaining buffered values first, and only exits once the channel is both closed and fully drained.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both `ch <- 1` and `ch <- 2` succeed immediately with no receiver present, because the channel's buffer has capacity 2 and neither send exceeds it. `close(ch)` marks the channel as closed for any further sends, but it does not erase or invalidate the two values already sitting in the buffer -- `for v := range ch` continues to receive them in order (1, then 2) exactly as if the channel were still open, and only exits the loop once the buffer is empty and the channel is closed, which the range loop detects automatically without you needing to check the two-value `ok` form by hand. The final print then runs normally, since nothing here panics or blocks forever -- closing a channel that still has buffered values is completely legitimate and a common pattern for 'no more values are coming, but drain whatever's left first.'

exercises.prompt: This program is supposed to collect results from 3 worker goroutines into a slice and print them, but it hangs forever instead of finishing. Find and fix the bug.
hints: `for v := range results` only stops once `results` is closed. Does anything in this program ever call close(results)?
Each worker sends exactly once and then returns -- nobody is left with a responsibility to close the channel once all 3 sends have happened.

You need some way to know when all 3 workers are done, so you can close the channel exactly once, after all sends -- consider a sync.WaitGroup combined with a separate goroutine that waits on it and then closes the channel.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code's `for v := range results` will only ever stop once `results` is closed, but nothing in the program ever calls `close(results)` -- each worker sends its one value and returns, and nobody takes responsibility for closing the channel afterward, so `range` keeps waiting for a 4th value that will never arrive, hanging forever (main is still making progress in the sense that it's not deadlocked-and-crashed, since the workers did successfully send and main did successfully receive 3 values -- it's just stuck waiting on a channel that was never told 'no more are coming'). The fix adds a `sync.WaitGroup` so something can know exactly when all 3 workers have finished sending, and a separate goroutine that calls `wg.Wait()` and then `close(results)` -- closing exactly once, only after every worker's send has actually completed. That close is what lets the `range` loop in main correctly exit once all 3 values have been drained, rather than waiting indefinitely for one that will never come.

assessments.prompt: Why does Go's `select` statement pick randomly among multiple ready cases, rather than always choosing the first ready case in source-code order?
options: It's an unavoidable limitation of how the Go runtime schedules goroutines, not a deliberate design choice.
Randomizing improves raw performance by letting the runtime skip checking later cases once an earlier one is found ready.

It's a deliberate design choice that prevents code from accidentally depending on the order cases happen to be written in, forcing each case to be treated as genuinely independent rather than implicitly prioritized.
It only picks randomly when exactly two cases are ready; with three or more ready cases, it always picks the first one in source order.
assessments.explanation: Go's select statement is explicitly specified to choose uniformly at random among whichever cases are ready at the moment it evaluates them, precisely so that developers can't accidentally write code that only works because case A happens to be listed before case B -- every case must be written as if it could be the one chosen, regardless of position. Option A is wrong -- this is a specified language behavior, not an incidental scheduling quirk. Option B is wrong and actually describes the opposite of what happens -- picking randomly among all ready cases requires checking all of them, not stopping early. Option D is wrong -- there's no special-casing based on the number of ready cases; the same random-choice rule applies uniformly regardless of how many cases happen to be ready.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between a full-program deadlock and a goroutine leak in Go, and why Go's runtime can detect and crash on one but not the other.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both involve a goroutine blocked forever on an operation -- typically a channel send or receive -- that will never be completed by anything else. The difference is scope: a full-program deadlock is specifically the situation where every single goroutine in the entire program is simultaneously blocked, with no goroutine anywhere left running that could possibly unblock any of the others -- the whole program has come to a complete, permanent stop. Go's runtime actively monitors for exactly this global condition, and when it detects that literally nothing is runnable anywhere, it crashes the program immediately with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!' rather than hanging silently forever, which is a real kindness during development since it surfaces the bug loudly and immediately instead of leaving you staring at a program that just never returns. A goroutine leak, by contrast, is a partial condition: one or more goroutines are permanently stuck, but the rest of the program -- including main, and possibly many other goroutines -- keeps making real, ongoing progress. Because the program as a whole is not stuck, the runtime's deadlock detector has nothing to trigger on; from its point of view, things are fine, since at least one goroutine somewhere is still runnable. This is exactly why leaks are more dangerous in practice than full deadlocks: a deadlock announces itself loudly and immediately during testing or even production, forcing a fix, while a leak can silently accumulate stuck goroutines one at a time -- often triggered by a specific, maybe rare, error-handling code path -- for hours or days in a long-running service, slowly consuming memory, until it eventually degrades or crashes the process with no clear, single, reproducible trigger to point at.

concepts.title: The sync Package: Mutex and WaitGroup
concepts.description: sync.Mutex protects shared state from concurrent access, and sync.WaitGroup lets one goroutine wait for a group of others to finish -- the two most common tools for coordinating goroutines when a channel isn't the natural fit.
learningObjectives: Explain what a data race is and why concurrent unsynchronized access to shared memory is undefined behavior in Go, not merely 'probably fine.'
Use sync.Mutex (Lock/Unlock) to protect a shared variable from concurrent access, including with defer.
Use sync.WaitGroup (Add/Done/Wait) to wait for a known number of goroutines to finish.
Explain why forgetting to call wg.Add before launching a goroutine (or calling it inside the goroutine) is a race condition in itself.
Run the race detector (`go run -race`) and explain what kind of bug it actually catches.

sections.heading: Data Races: Why Unsynchronized Shared Access Is Genuinely Undefined
sections.body:
A **data race** occurs when two or more goroutines access the same memory location concurrently, at least one of those accesses is a write, and there's no synchronization ordering one access relative to the other. This is worth taking seriously as more than a vague warning: in Go, a data race is **undefined behavior** -- not merely 'you might get a slightly stale value,' but a genuine correctness violation that the language specification explicitly does not define the outcome of. The Go memory model does not guarantee you'll simply see 'the old value' or 'the new value'; on real hardware, a data race on anything larger than a single machine word can produce a torn, nonsensical value that was never actually written by anyone -- a mix of bytes from two different writes.

```go
counter := 0
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 1000; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		counter++   // DATA RACE: read-modify-write with no synchronization
	}()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(counter)   // frequently NOT 1000 -- often some smaller number, and it varies run to run
```

`counter++` is not a single atomic operation -- it's read the current value, add one, write it back, three distinct steps. When two goroutines interleave those steps (goroutine A reads 5, goroutine B also reads 5 before A writes back, both compute 6, both write 6 -- one increment is silently lost), the final count ends up lower than 1000, and by how much varies unpredictably from run to run. This exact bug is the textbook motivating example for the tools in this concept.

sections.heading: sync.Mutex: Mutual Exclusion
sections.body:
A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) ensures that only one goroutine at a time can execute the section of code between a `Lock()` and its matching `Unlock()` -- any other goroutine calling `Lock()` while it's already held simply blocks until the holder calls `Unlock()`. This turns the unsafe `counter++` above into something genuinely safe:

```go
var (
	counter int
	mu      sync.Mutex
)

func increment() {
	mu.Lock()
	defer mu.Unlock()
	counter++
}
```

`defer mu.Unlock()` immediately after `mu.Lock()` is close to a fixed idiom in Go, and it's worth understanding exactly why: it guarantees the unlock happens no matter how the function exits -- including via an early `return`, or even a `panic` unwinding through the function. Without `defer`, a function with multiple return paths or the possibility of panicking would need to remember to call `Unlock()` on every single one of those paths, and missing even one leaves the mutex permanently locked -- every other goroutine that ever tries to `Lock()` it again blocks forever, effectively becoming a self-inflicted deadlock (or, more precisely, a goroutine leak affecting every future caller). Recall from the Structs and Methods concept that `sync.Mutex`'s zero value is already a valid, unlocked mutex -- `var mu sync.Mutex` needs no constructor -- which is exactly why you'll see it declared as a plain struct field with no initialization step anywhere.

One more rule worth stating explicitly: **a `sync.Mutex` (like most sync types) must never be copied after first use.** If a struct contains a `sync.Mutex` field, pass that struct around by pointer, not by value -- copying it duplicates the lock's internal state, and the copy no longer actually protects the same critical section as the original, silently defeating the whole point of having a mutex at all. `go vet` will catch some, but not all, cases of this mistake.

sections.heading: sync.WaitGroup: Waiting for a Known Number of Goroutines
sections.body:
`sync.WaitGroup` solves a different, extremely common problem: 'launch N goroutines, and don't proceed until all N have finished.' It has exactly three methods that matter: `Add(n)` increments an internal counter by `n`; `Done()` decrements it by 1 (and is equivalent to `Add(-1)`); `Wait()` blocks until that counter reaches zero.

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func(id int) {
		defer wg.Done()
		fmt.Println("worker", id, "running")
	}(i)
}
wg.Wait()   // blocks until all 5 workers have called Done()
fmt.Println("all workers finished")
```

The placement of `wg.Add(1)` matters more than it might look like at first glance: it must happen in the goroutine that is *launching* the new goroutine, **before** the `go` statement -- never inside the new goroutine itself. If `Add` were called inside the goroutine, there would be a race between that `Add` actually executing and the main goroutine reaching `wg.Wait()`: if `Wait()` runs before any goroutine gets around to calling its own `Add(1)`, the counter could still be at zero, and `Wait()` would return immediately, believing (incorrectly) that there's nothing left to wait for, even though goroutines are still queued up or newly starting. Calling `Add` in the launching goroutine, before `go`, guarantees the counter reflects every goroutine that's about to run before `Wait()` has any chance to check it.

`defer wg.Done()` at the very top of the goroutine's body mirrors the `defer mu.Unlock()` idiom for exactly the same reason: it guarantees `Done()` fires no matter how that goroutine's body exits, including through an early return or a panic -- and a missed `Done()` call means the counter never reaches zero, so `wg.Wait()` blocks forever, another concrete way to accidentally manufacture a goroutine leak (this time affecting the waiting goroutine itself, not just the one that failed to call Done).

sections.heading: Mutex vs. Channel: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.body:
Go famously offers two different-feeling coordination styles -- channels (share memory by communicating) and the sync package (traditional locking) -- and it's worth having a working intuition for when each fits more naturally, rather than treating it as an arbitrary style choice. As a rough guideline: reach for a **mutex** when you have a piece of shared *state* -- a counter, a cache, a map -- that multiple goroutines need to read and mutate directly, and the natural unit of work is 'briefly touch this shared data structure and move on.' Reach for a **channel** when you're coordinating the *flow* of values or signals between goroutines -- handing off work items, fanning results back in, signaling completion or cancellation -- where the interesting thing is the handoff itself, not a piece of state sitting still that many goroutines poke at.

These aren't mutually exclusive, and idiomatic Go code frequently uses both together -- a worker pool might use channels to distribute jobs and collect results, while a mutex-protected map inside one of those workers tracks some running statistic. Neither tool is 'more advanced' or 'more idiomatic' than the other in some absolute sense; picking based on which one matches the actual shape of the coordination problem, rather than defaulting to whichever one you learned first, is the actual skill.

sections.heading: The Race Detector: A Tool, Not a Guess
sections.body:
Data races are notoriously hard to catch by simply running a program and looking at its output, because a race might only manifest under specific timing that doesn't reliably occur on your machine, in your test run, today. Go ships with a built-in **race detector**, enabled with the `-race` flag on `go run`, `go build`, or `go test`: `go run -race main.go`. It instruments memory accesses at runtime and watches for genuinely unsynchronized concurrent access to the same memory location, reporting the exact goroutines, stack traces, and memory addresses involved the moment it observes one -- rather than requiring you to somehow spot a wrong final number and reverse-engineer where the race must be coming from.

It's worth being precise about what `-race` actually guarantees: it can only detect races that **actually occur during that specific run** -- if the particular interleaving that triggers a race doesn't happen to occur while the instrumented program is running (because the buggy code path wasn't exercised, or the timing didn't line up that time), `-race` reports nothing, even though the race is still latent in the code and could surface on a different run, a different machine, or under different load. This means a clean `-race` run is meaningful evidence, not a mathematical proof of race-freedom -- running your test suite with `-race` regularly (many teams enable it permanently in CI) substantially increases the odds of catching races before production, but it is not, and cannot be, an absolute guarantee for code paths a given run didn't actually exercise.

examples.title: The Unsynchronized Counter Race, and the Mutex Fix
examples.explanation: Every one of the 1000 goroutines now acquires `mu` before touching `counter`, and releases it immediately afterward via `defer mu.Unlock()` -- so the read-increment-write sequence inside `counter++` can never be interrupted by another goroutine partway through; whichever goroutine holds the lock completes its full read-modify-write cycle before any other goroutine's `Lock()` call is allowed to proceed. This is the difference between the earlier unsynchronized version (which frequently under-counts, and by a different amount each run, due to lost updates from interleaved reads and writes) and this version, which reliably prints exactly 1000 on every single run, because the mutex has eliminated the possibility of that interleaving entirely. `wg.Add(1)` before each `go func()` and `defer wg.Done()` as the first line of each goroutine together guarantee `wg.Wait()` doesn't return until literally all 1000 goroutines have finished incrementing.

examples.title: The wg.Add Placement Bug
examples.explanation: `wg.Add(1)` is called from inside each newly-launched goroutine rather than by the loop, before `go func(id int) {...}(i)` starts it. This creates a race between the main goroutine reaching `wg.Wait()` and each launched goroutine actually getting scheduled and executing its own `wg.Add(1)` -- if `Wait()` happens to run before any goroutine has called `Add`, the WaitGroup's internal counter is still 0, and `Wait()` returns immediately, believing there's nothing to wait for, even though 5 goroutines are about to run (or are mid-flight) and will append to `results` afterward. The result is that `len(results)` printed by main is unreliable -- it might occasionally be 5 if scheduling happens to work out, but frequently prints fewer, and the exact number varies unpredictably run to run. The fix is always to call `wg.Add(1)` in the loop itself, immediately before each `go` statement, so the counter correctly reflects every goroutine about to be launched before `Wait()` ever has a chance to check it.

examples.title: Passing a Mutex-Containing Struct by Pointer, Not Value
examples.explanation: `counter` is a `*SafeCounter` (a pointer), created directly with `&SafeCounter{}`, and every one of the 100 goroutines calls `Increment()` on that same underlying struct through that same pointer -- so all 100 calls are contending for, and correctly synchronized by, the exact same `mu`. This matters specifically because `sync.Mutex` must never be copied after use: if `Increment` had a value receiver (`func (c SafeCounter) Increment()`), each call would receive its own independent copy of the entire struct -- including a copy of `mu` -- meaning every goroutine would be locking and unlocking its own private, freshly-copied mutex that has nothing to do with any other goroutine's copy, providing zero actual protection for the real, shared `count` field (which, being copied too, wouldn't even be the field other goroutines see anyway). The pointer receiver is what makes this whole pattern correct: every goroutine reaches the same struct, the same mutex, and the same count field, rather than each getting its own disconnected copy.

misconceptions.description: A data race in Go just means you might occasionally read a slightly outdated value -- annoying, but generally harmless, similar to eventual consistency in a distributed system.
misconceptions.clarification: A data race is genuine undefined behavior in the Go memory model, not merely a staleness issue. The language specification makes no guarantee at all about what value a racing read observes -- it is not guaranteed to be 'the old value' or 'the new value'; on real hardware, for values larger than a single machine word, a race can produce a torn value that was never actually written by any goroutine at all, a corrupted mix of bytes from two separate writes. Beyond incorrect values, the Go compiler is also permitted to apply optimizations that assume the absence of data races, meaning racy code can behave in ways that seem to defy the program's literal source order entirely. Treating a known data race as 'probably fine most of the time' is a real correctness bug waiting to surface unpredictably, not a harmless staleness trade-off.

misconceptions.description: It doesn't matter whether `wg.Add(1)` is called just before launching a goroutine or as the first line inside that goroutine -- either way, the counter gets incremented before the goroutine finishes, so wg.Wait() will work correctly.
misconceptions.clarification: It matters a great deal, because of when `wg.Wait()` might be called relative to when the goroutine actually gets scheduled and starts running. If `Add(1)` is called inside the goroutine rather than by the launching code before `go`, there's a window where the goroutine has been started but hasn't yet run far enough to call its own `Add(1)` -- and if the launching goroutine reaches `wg.Wait()` during exactly that window, it sees a counter that hasn't been incremented yet, may already be zero, and returns immediately, incorrectly believing there's nothing left to wait for. Calling `Add(1)` in the launching code, immediately before the `go` statement, guarantees the counter reflects that goroutine's existence before `Wait()` could possibly be reached, eliminating that race entirely.

exercises.prompt: Will this program reliably print 500 every time it's run? Explain why or why not.
hints: wg.Add/Done/Wait correctly ensures main waits for all 500 goroutines to finish -- but does that alone protect `total` itself from concurrent access?
`total++` is a read-modify-write operation involving 3 separate steps, not one atomic step. What happens if two goroutines' steps interleave?
sync.WaitGroup solves the 'wait for completion' problem; it does nothing at all to protect shared data from being read and written concurrently -- that's a separate concern requiring a separate tool.
exercises.expectedAnswer: No -- it will frequently print something less than 500, and the exact number will vary from run to run. wg correctly waits for all 500 goroutines to finish, but total++ is a data race: nothing synchronizes access to `total` itself, so concurrent read-modify-write interleavings across goroutines cause some increments to be silently lost.
exercises.solutionExplanation: sync.WaitGroup only tracks and signals completion -- it guarantees wg.Wait() doesn't return until all 500 goroutines have called wg.Done(), but it provides zero protection for any shared data those goroutines touch along the way. `total++` expands to a read, an addition, and a write, and with no mutex or other synchronization guarding `total`, two goroutines can interleave those steps: both read the same current value, both independently compute value+1, and both write back the same result, silently losing one of the two increments. Across 500 goroutines racing like this, some number of increments get lost this way, so the final total is frequently below 500 -- and because the exact interleaving depends on unpredictable scheduling, the specific shortfall varies from run to run rather than being a fixed, reproducible number. Fixing this requires wrapping `total++` in a sync.Mutex Lock/Unlock (or using sync/atomic for a simple counter like this), entirely separate from the WaitGroup, which is solving a different problem.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to safely record scores from multiple goroutines into a shared map, but it panics with 'concurrent map writes' (or occasionally 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write'). Find and fix the bug.
hints: Go's built-in map type is explicitly documented as NOT safe for concurrent use without extra synchronization -- multiple goroutines writing to the same map at the same time is a real, detected-at-runtime problem, not just a data race that silently loses data.
sync.WaitGroup here correctly waits for all 5 goroutines to finish, but does nothing to serialize their access to the shared `scores` map while they're running.
Add a sync.Mutex, and Lock it around each goroutine's access to the map -- Lock immediately before the map write, Unlock (ideally via defer) immediately after.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Go's built-in map type is explicitly not safe for concurrent access -- the runtime actively detects concurrent writes (and concurrent read/write mixes) to the same map and crashes immediately with a fatal error, rather than silently corrupting data or quietly losing entries. `sync.WaitGroup` in the original code correctly ensures main waits for all 5 goroutines to finish, but it does absolutely nothing to prevent those 5 goroutines from writing into `scores` at the same moment as each other, which is exactly what triggers the panic. The fix introduces a `sync.Mutex`, locked immediately before each goroutine's map write and unlocked (via `defer`) immediately after -- this serializes access to `scores` so that only one goroutine is ever actually writing into the map at any given instant, eliminating the concurrent-access condition the runtime was detecting and crashing on.

assessments.prompt: A team lead says: 'We ran the program under `go run -race` for an hour and it reported nothing, so I'm confident this code has no data races anywhere.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: The race detector only works on code that uses channels, not sync.Mutex, so it wouldn't have caught mutex-related races anyway.

The race detector can only report races that actually occur during the instrumented run -- if a particular buggy interleaving or code path wasn't exercised during that hour, it produces no warning, even though the race may still be latent in the code.
The -race flag only checks for races in the first few seconds of program execution, then stops monitoring to save overhead.
go run -race doesn't actually detect data races at all -- it only detects full-program deadlocks.
assessments.explanation: The race detector instruments actual memory accesses during a real execution and reports races it genuinely observes -- but it cannot report a race whose triggering interleaving or code path simply didn't happen to occur during that specific run. A clean hour-long run is meaningful evidence that no race was triggered under that particular load and timing, not a proof that the code is race-free under all possible timings, inputs, and schedules. Option A is wrong -- the race detector works on any memory access, including those protected (or unprotected) by sync.Mutex, not just channel operations. Option C is wrong -- there's no such time-limited monitoring window; it runs for the duration of the instrumented program. Option D is wrong -- data race detection is precisely -race's core purpose; full deadlock detection is a separate, always-on runtime feature that doesn't require the -race flag at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain why sync.WaitGroup and sync.Mutex solve two genuinely different problems, using an example where a program might correctly use one but still be buggy without the other.
assessments.modelAnswer: sync.WaitGroup solves a completion-tracking problem: it lets one goroutine know when a specific, known number of other goroutines have all finished running, via Add to register expected work, Done to mark one unit of work complete, and Wait to block until the count returns to zero. It says nothing whatsoever about what those goroutines do to shared data while they're running, or whether their accesses to that data are safe relative to each other -- it purely tracks 'how many are still in flight.' sync.Mutex solves a completely different problem: mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one goroutine at a time can execute a particular section of code -- typically a section that reads or writes some piece of shared state -- so that concurrent accesses can't interleave in a way that corrupts or loses data. A concrete example that uses WaitGroup correctly but is still buggy without a Mutex: spinning up 1000 goroutines that each increment a shared `int` counter, wrapped correctly with wg.Add(1) before each launch and defer wg.Done() inside each goroutine, then calling wg.Wait() in main. The WaitGroup usage is entirely correct here -- main really will wait until all 1000 goroutines have finished running before it proceeds. But without a mutex (or an equivalent, like sync/atomic) protecting the counter's read-modify-write increment, those 1000 goroutines can still race on the counter itself, causing some increments to be silently lost due to interleaved reads and writes, so the final printed count frequently comes out below 1000, varying by run. The program 'waits correctly' thanks to WaitGroup while simultaneously producing a wrong answer due to the missing Mutex -- which is exactly the point: one tool answers 'has everyone finished,' the other answers 'is it safe for everyone to touch this data at once,' and a program can get either one right while still getting the other wrong.
